title: Managing Images: Pull, List, Remove 🖼️
description: Pull images from Docker Hub, inspect them, and clean up your local image cache.

slides.title: Pulling Images from a Registry 📥
slides.content:
# `docker pull` – Getting the Goods

Images live on **registries** (like Docker Hub). To download an image locally, use `docker pull`:

```bash
docker pull <image>:<tag>
```

- `<image>` – the repository name (e.g., `nginx`, `python`, `ubuntu`)
- `<tag>` – a version label; defaults to `latest` if omitted.

**Examples:**
```bash
docker pull nginx          # pulls nginx:latest
docker pull python:3.11    # pulls Python version 3.11
```

> `latest` doesn’t mean “newest” – it’s just the default tag. Always pin exact versions in production!

slides.title: Pull in Action 👇
slides.content: Pull a small Alpine Linux image to see what happens:

quizData.question: What happens if you run `docker pull node` without specifying a tag?

options.text: It fails because a tag is required.
It pulls the most recently uploaded version.

quizData.explanation: If no tag is specified, Docker uses `latest` by default. It's important to know that `latest` is just a tag, not the actual latest version.

slides.title: Listing Local Images 📋
slides.content:
# `docker images` / `docker image ls`

To see what images you already have on your machine:

```bash
docker images
# or
 docker image ls
```

Output columns:
- **REPOSITORY** – image name
- **TAG** – version label
- **IMAGE ID** – unique SHA256 hash
- **CREATED** – when the image was built
- **SIZE** – total size on disk

slides.title: Sample Image List 📊
slides.content: After pulling a few images, your output might look like:
slides.codeSnippet:
REPOSITORY   TAG       IMAGE ID       CREATED        SIZE
alpine       3.18      5e2b554c1c45   2 weeks ago    7.33MB
nginx        latest    ac232364af82   3 weeks ago    142MB
hello-world  latest    feb5d9fea6a5   5 months ago   13.3kB

quizData.question: What does the IMAGE ID represent?

options.text: A unique identifier (SHA256 hash) for the image.
The name of the registry it came from.
The size of the image in bytes.

quizData.explanation: Each image has a unique ID (a cryptographic hash). You can reference an image by its ID or by name:tag.

slides.title: Removing Images 🗑️
slides.content:
# `docker rmi` / `docker image rm`

Free up disk space by deleting images you no longer need.

```bash
docker rmi <image>
```

- You can use the **image name:tag** or the **IMAGE ID**.
- You cannot remove an image if any container (even stopped) is using it. Stop and remove those containers first, or use `-f` to force.

**Examples:**
```bash
docker rmi alpine:3.18
docker rmi 5e2b554c1c45   # using IMAGE ID
```

quizData.question: You can delete an image even if a container created from it is still running.
quizData.explanation: Docker prevents deletion of images that are in use by any container (running or stopped) unless you force it with `-f`. Best practice is to stop and remove containers first.

slides.title: Dangling Images 👻
slides.content:
## What Are Dangling Images?
After you build or pull newer versions, old untagged images may become “dangling” (their repository and tag show `<none>`). Use:
```bash
docker image prune
```
to remove them all in one go.
